summary: Defines OSPF extensions that let a Path Computation Client automatically find Path Computation Elements and learn what they can do. This helps when the PCE participates in the IGP. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Routers needing help planning routes can ask around who the planners are. This lets OSPF announce which servers are route planners and what they are good at.

subtitle: How OSPF routers announce which of them can compute paths for others, and what kinds of paths they can compute.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client needs to find the Path Computation Elements it can ask, and learn enough about each to choose one, without manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: A PCE advertises a PCE Discovery (PCED) TLV, type 6, inside an OSPF Router Information LSA. Sub-TLVs give its address, path scope and preferences, domains and capability flags.
tldr.outcome: PCCs in an OSPF domain can find PCEs and notice new, failed or changed ones through normal OSPF flooding. RFC 9353 updates this document.

today: RFC 5088 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008 and is updated by RFC 9353. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Discovery Problem
sections.content:
In the PCE architecture (RFC 4655) a Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths for MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineered label switched paths, and a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks it to. A network may hold many PCEs with different abilities, so a PCC needs a way to find them automatically and to notice new PCEs, failed PCEs or changed PCE information. The requirements are in RFC 4674.

When PCCs and PCEs take part in the IGP, the RFC says IGP advertisements are an effective way to do this. This document defines OSPF extensions for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. It builds on the generic capability advertisement of RFC 4970 by adding a new TLV, the PCED TLV, to the OSPF Router Information LSA.

Two things are out of scope: how a PCC picks among the PCEs it finds, and discovery across Autonomous System boundaries, which is left for further study. IS-IS has a companion document, RFC 5089.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school where some students are good at planning routes for field trips. This gives everyone a way to find those students without asking each person.

sections.title: What Gets Advertised and Where It Floods
sections.content:
The discovery information has five parts: the PCE location (an IPv4 and/or IPv6 address), the path computation scope (intra-area, inter-area, inter-AS or inter-layer), the PCE-Domains it can see, the neighbor PCE-Domains it can compute toward, and its communication and path computation capabilities.

This information is fairly static. It changes with configuration, activation, deactivation or failure, so it is not expected to change often.

The flooding scope can be limited to one or more OSPF areas the PCE belongs to, or extended to the entire OSPF routing domain. A PCE in several areas, such as an Area Border Router, could advertise in the backbone area and some of its attached areas.
sections.eli5: A route-planning helper puts up a poster saying where to find them, which kinds of trips they can plan, and what tools they have. The poster is shown to one neighborhood or the whole town.

sections.title: The PCED TLV and Its Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The PCED TLV uses the same TLV format as RFC 3630: a 2-octet type, a 2-octet length and a value, padded to 4-octet alignment without counting the padding in the length. Its type is 6 and its value is a set of sub-TLVs in no particular order.

Five sub-TLVs exist. PCE-ADDRESS and PATH-SCOPE MUST always be present. PCE-DOMAIN, NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN and PCE-CAP-FLAGS are optional. Unknown sub-TLVs MUST be silently ignored, while a malformed PCED TLV makes the LSA malformed under normal OSPF rules. The RFC states that no more sub-TLVs will be added in the future.

  • PCE-ADDRESS holds an address-type (1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6) and the address. It may appear twice when the PCE has both kinds, and only the first of a given type is used. An always-reachable address is RECOMMENDED.
  • PCE-DOMAIN names an area (domain-type 1) or an AS number (domain-type 2) where the PCE has visibility. It SHOULD be present when the domains cannot be inferred from other IGP information.
  • NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN has the same format and names a neighbor area or AS toward which the PCE can compute paths.
  • PCE-CAP-FLAGS is an array of 32-bit flags, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero. IANA manages the space.
sections.eli5: The poster is made of labeled boxes. Two boxes are always needed, where to find the planner and what kind of trips it plans. The others are extras, and a reader who does not know a box just skips it.

sections.title: Path Scope, Preferences and Capabilities
sections.content:
The PATH-SCOPE sub-TLV has exactly one instance per PCED TLV. It has six flag bits: L (intra-area), R (inter-area), Rd (default PCE for inter-area), S (inter-AS), Sd (default PCE for inter-AS) and Y (inter-layer). The L, R, S and Y bits are non-exclusive. A default PCE can compute a path toward any neighbor domain. When Rd and Sd are set, the PCED TLV MUST NOT contain a NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN sub-TLV. If R is set and Rd is clear, a NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN with domain-type 1 MUST be present, and likewise domain-type 2 for S and Sd.

Four 3-bit preference fields, PrefL, PrefR, PrefS and PrefY, rank the PCE for each scope, where 7 is the highest. They can be used for weighted load balancing. How a PCC actually balances its requests is left to local or network-wide policy.

The PCE-CAP-FLAGS bits assigned by IANA, defined in RFC 4657, cover capabilities such as bidirectional path computation, diverse path computation and request prioritization.
sections.eli5: The planner says which kinds of trips it can plan, and gives each kind a score from 0 to 7 for how much it wants that work. That helps spread the work out evenly.

sections.title: Flooding and Lifecycle Rules
sections.content:
The PCED TLV travels in an OSPFv2 Router Information LSA (Opaque type 4, Opaque ID 0) or an OSPFv3 Router Information LSA (function code 12), and otherwise follows the procedures of RFC 4970. For an area-local scope it MUST go in an OSPFv2 type 10 LSA, or in OSPFv3 with S1 set and S2 clear. For the whole routing domain it MUST go in a type 11 LSA, or OSPFv3 with S1 clear and S2 set. If only the L bit is set, the scope MUST be area local.

When a PCE is deactivated, its OSPF speaker MUST originate a new Router Information LSA without the PCED TLV, or send an empty LSA or purge it if no other TLVs remain. Any change in PCE state MUST be reflected in the advertised TLV. The advertiser must itself be reachable via OSPF paths in the same area for the information to count as current, and a change in the TLV MUST NOT trigger an SPF computation at a receiving router.

For backward compatibility, a router that does not support the PCED TLV silently ignores it, so no interoperability issues arise.
sections.eli5: When the planner retires, it replaces its poster with one that leaves it out. And putting up a new poster does not make everyone redo their whole map.

sections.title: Manageability and Network Impact
sections.content:
Manageability follows Section 4.10 of RFC 4674. A PCE implementation SHOULD allow configuring its addresses, scope and preferences, PCE-Domains, neighbor PCE-Domains and capabilities. A MIB module for PCE Discovery is referenced as a work in progress, and normal OSPF operation satisfies the liveness detection requirement.

Frequent changes to the advertised information could destabilize the network by making PCCs swap between PCEs. So it MUST be possible to apply controls: a configurable limit on how fast a PCE announces changes, rate-limiting of PCED TLV processing at PCCs, and configurable triggers for a PCC to move to another PCE.
sections.eli5: If the planners kept changing their posters every minute, everyone would keep switching helpers. So there are limits on how often posters can change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines discovery within an administrative domain, so its security relies on the security of OSPF. Mechanisms that protect the authenticity and integrity of LSAs and their TLVs, such as those in RFC 2154, can protect the PCE discovery information too.

OSPF provides no encryption, so the privacy of LSAs, and therefore of the PCE discovery information, is not protected.
sections.eli5: The posters are as safe as the notice board they hang on. Anyone who can read the board can read the posters.
